title: Reading a profile of someone with an unusual job

objective.en: Read a magazine profile of someone with an unusual job and find the facts, her attitude to the work and the writer’s purpose in telling her story.
objective.fr: Lire le portrait d’une personne au métier insolite et trouver les faits, son attitude face au travail et l’intention de l’auteur.
objective.de: Ein Magazinporträt über einen ungewöhnlichen Beruf lesen und Fakten, die Haltung zur Arbeit und die Absicht des Autors erkennen.

documents.title: The Woman Who Keeps Time
paragraphs: Every Monday at seven in the morning, Ruth Calder climbs 212 steps to the top of the cathedral tower in Wexbridge. Nobody tells her to hurry. She has a heavy brass key in her pocket, a torch in her hand and, above her head, a clock that has been ticking since 1887.

Ruth is one of the last clock keepers in the country. Her job is to wind the mechanism by hand, oil every wheel and make sure the clock is never more than a few seconds wrong. It is slow, painstaking work, and she has done it for twenty-six years.

She did not plan this life. Ruth trained as an accountant and spent her twenties staring at spreadsheets. Then, on a walk, she heard the cathedral bells and asked the vicar if she could see the machinery. Within a year she had given up her office job. ‘It was never a career,’ she says. ‘It was a vocation. I simply could not walk away.’

The work is not glamorous. The tower is cold in winter and unbearably hot in summer, and the pay is modest. Her trade is also dwindling, because most towns now use electric clocks that need no care at all. Yet Ruth never complains. She has a knack for hearing when something is wrong: a tiny change in the rhythm tells her a bearing is dry long before it fails.

Visitors sometimes ask whether she is lonely up there. Ruth laughs. ‘I have the best view in town, and a clock for company,’ she says. ‘Most days I feel I am the only person who notices the time passing. Everyone else looks at their phones.’

Ruth’s story matters because it reminds us how much skilled work goes unnoticed. Next time you glance at a town clock, remember that somebody climbed those steps to keep it honest. Her successor, a nervous teenager called Sam, starts training in April. Ruth is already teaching him to listen.

documents.title: Naming the Colours
paragraphs: Last year, Tomás Ibarra gave names to 340 shades of paint. ‘Dusty Biscuit’ is his. So is ‘Tuesday Rain’. He works from a tiny studio above a bakery, where he spends his days staring at small squares of colour and waiting for a phrase to arrive.

Friends find the job hilarious, and Tomás does not mind. He studied literature and wrote poetry for a decade before a paint company advertised the post. ‘A good name should make you feel something before you have even opened the tin,’ he says. ‘Grey is just grey. But Morning Fog makes you want to stay in bed.’

Not everything is poetic, though. Tomás must check that no name is already taken, and that none sounds rude in another language. Last month a colour he loved, ‘Sunday Mud’, was rejected because another company already used it. He shrugged and moved on to the next square.

items.question: Why has the writer chosen to write about Ruth Calder?

options.text: To encourage readers to train as clock keepers
To argue that electric clocks should be banned
To show how much skilled work people fail to notice
To warn that the cathedral tower is unsafe

answerExplanation.en: The final paragraph states the point: her story reminds us how much skilled work goes unnoticed.
answerExplanation.fr: Le dernier paragraphe donne l’idée : son histoire nous rappelle combien de travail qualifié passe inaperçu.
answerExplanation.de: Der letzte Absatz nennt die Absicht: Ihre Geschichte erinnert uns daran, wie viel qualifizierte Arbeit unbemerkt bleibt.

items.question: What made Ruth leave her office job?

options.text: The vicar offered her a higher salary
Her company closed down

She wanted to travel after her twenties

answerExplanation.de: Auf einem Spaziergang hörte sie die Glocken, wollte das Uhrwerk sehen und hatte binnen eines Jahres gekündigt.

items.question: How does Ruth feel about the difficulties of her job?

options.text: She regrets leaving accountancy
She hopes to find an easier job
She blames the cathedral for the low pay
She accepts them without complaining

answerExplanation.fr: L’auteur écrit « Yet Ruth never complains » malgré le froid, la chaleur et le salaire modeste.
answerExplanation.de: Der Autor schreibt „Yet Ruth never complains“ trotz Kälte, Hitze und bescheidener Bezahlung.

items.statement: Ruth finds the tower a lonely place to work.

answerExplanation.en: False: she laughs at the question and says she has the best view in town and a clock for company.

answerExplanation.de: Falsch: Sie lacht über die Frage und sagt, sie habe die beste Aussicht der Stadt und eine Uhr als Gesellschaft.

items.question: What is the writer’s main aim in this profile?

options.text: To persuade readers to repaint their homes
To show that an unusual job mixes creativity with practical limits
To criticise companies that invent colour names
To explain how paint is made

answerExplanation.en: The profile shows his poetic side (‘Morning Fog’) and the practical limits: names already taken or sounding rude in another language.
answerExplanation.fr: Le portrait montre son côté poétique (« Morning Fog ») et les limites pratiques : noms déjà pris ou grossiers dans une autre langue.
answerExplanation.de: Das Porträt zeigt seine poetische Seite („Morning Fog“) und die praktischen Grenzen: bereits vergebene oder in anderen Sprachen unpassende Namen.
